lessons.title: Introduction to DBMS and Database Architecture
lessons.description: Understand database management systems, relational databases, keys and database architecture.
lessons.content:
A Database Management System (DBMS) is software used to store, organize, retrieve, update and manage data efficiently.

Examples include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and MongoDB. MongoDB is a document-oriented database, while MySQL and PostgreSQL are relational database management systems.

DBMS advantages:
1. Reduces unnecessary data duplication.
2. Supports data integrity.
3. Provides controlled data access.
4. Supports concurrent users.
5. Enables backup and recovery.
6. Supports efficient queries.

DBMS vs RDBMS:
A DBMS is a broad category of database management software. An RDBMS is a DBMS based on the relational model, which represents data through relations, commonly implemented as tables.

Example Student table:
StudentID | Name | Department
101 | Rahul | MCA
102 | Priya | MBA
103 | Arjun | MCA

Important terminology:
Table: Collection of rows and columns.
Row: A record or tuple.
Column: An attribute.
Schema: Logical definition of database structures.
Instance: Actual data stored at a particular time.

Database keys:
Primary Key: Uniquely identifies a row and cannot contain NULL values.
Foreign Key: References a candidate or primary key in another or the same table, depending on the DBMS.
Candidate Key: Minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row.
Super Key: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row.
Composite Key: Key consisting of multiple attributes.
Alternate Key: Candidate key not selected as the primary key.

Example:
Students(StudentID, Name, DepartmentID)
Departments(DepartmentID, DepartmentName)

StudentID is the primary key of Students. DepartmentID can be a foreign key referencing Departments.

Three-schema architecture:
External Level: User-specific views.
Conceptual Level: Overall logical database structure.
Internal Level: Physical storage representation.

Data independence:
Logical data independence allows conceptual schema changes without requiring changes to external views when compatibility is preserved.
Physical data independence allows changes in physical storage without changing the conceptual schema.

Interview question: What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?

Answer: A primary key uniquely identifies records in its own table. A foreign key establishes a referential relationship with a key in another or the same table.

lessons.title: ER Model, Relationships and Normalization
lessons.description: Learn entity-relationship modeling, cardinality, functional dependencies and normalization.
lessons.content:
The Entity-Relationship (ER) model is used to design the logical structure of a database.

Entity: A distinguishable object such as Student, Course or Employee.
Attribute: A property of an entity, such as StudentID or Name.
Relationship: An association between entities.

Relationship cardinality:
One-to-One: One employee has one assigned locker, assuming the business rules enforce this relationship.
One-to-Many: One department has many employees.
Many-to-Many: Students enroll in multiple courses and courses contain multiple students.

Many-to-many relationships are commonly implemented using a junction table.

Example:
Students(StudentID, Name)
Courses(CourseID, CourseName)
Enrollments(StudentID, CourseID)

Normalization organizes relational tables to reduce redundancy and undesirable data dependencies.

Functional dependency:
A -> B means the value of A determines the value of B.

Example:
StudentID -> StudentName.

First Normal Form (1NF):
Each field contains a single value from its domain, and repeating groups are eliminated.

Second Normal Form (2NF):
The table is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key, eliminating partial dependencies.

Third Normal Form (3NF):
The table is in 2NF and, for every nontrivial functional dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute.

In common introductory examples, 3NF removes transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on a key.

Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF):
For every nontrivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.

Example of a normalization problem:
Enrollment(StudentID, StudentName, CourseID, CourseName)

If StudentID determines StudentName and CourseID determines CourseName, storing these values repeatedly creates redundancy.

A normalized design may use:
Students(StudentID, StudentName)
Courses(CourseID, CourseName)
Enrollments(StudentID, CourseID)

Database anomalies:
Insertion anomaly: Difficulty inserting information independently.
Update anomaly: Inconsistent data after partial updates.
Deletion anomaly: Losing unrelated information when deleting a record.

Interview question: Why is normalization important?

Answer: It reduces redundancy, improves consistency and helps prevent insertion, update and deletion anomalies.

Note: Normalization is a logical design technique. Denormalization may be deliberately used for performance when its trade-offs are understood.

lessons.title: SQL Concepts, Joins, Subqueries and Views
lessons.description: Review essential SQL operations and commonly asked DBMS interview queries.
lessons.content:
SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is used to define, query and manipulate relational database data.

Common SQL command categories:
DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.
DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
DQL: SELECT, often treated as a separate category in introductory materials.
DCL: GRANT, REVOKE.
TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.

Example:
CREATE TABLE Employees (
  EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  EmployeeName VARCHAR(100),
  Salary DECIMAL(10,2),
  DepartmentID INT
);

Retrieve all employees:
SELECT * FROM Employees;

Filter employees:
SELECT EmployeeName, Salary
FROM Employees
WHERE Salary > 50000;

Sort results:
SELECT * FROM Employees
ORDER BY Salary DESC;

Aggregate functions:
COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), MAX().

Example:
SELECT DepartmentID, AVG(Salary)
FROM Employees
GROUP BY DepartmentID;

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

Example:
SELECT DepartmentID, COUNT(*) AS EmployeeCount
FROM Employees
GROUP BY DepartmentID
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

SQL joins:
INNER JOIN: Returns rows satisfying the join condition.
LEFT JOIN: Preserves all left-side rows and matches right-side rows where available.
RIGHT JOIN: Preserves all right-side rows and matches left-side rows where available.
FULL OUTER JOIN: Preserves unmatched rows from both sides; availability and syntax vary by DBMS.
CROSS JOIN: Produces combinations of rows from both inputs.

Example:
SELECT e.EmployeeName, d.DepartmentName
FROM Employees e
INNER JOIN Departments d
ON e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID;

Subquery:
SELECT EmployeeName
FROM Employees
WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employees);

A view is a stored query definition that can be used like a virtual table. Some database systems also support materialized views that store query results.

Example:
CREATE VIEW HighSalaryEmployees AS
SELECT EmployeeID, EmployeeName, Salary
FROM Employees
WHERE Salary > 70000;

Important interview distinctions:
DELETE removes selected rows and can use WHERE.
TRUNCATE removes all rows from a table in systems supporting the statement, with transaction behavior varying by DBMS.
DROP removes a database object such as a table.

UNION combines result sets and removes duplicate rows.
UNION ALL combines result sets while retaining duplicates.

Interview tip: Be prepared to explain joins, grouping, subqueries and NULL handling with small examples.

lessons.title: Transactions, ACID Properties and Concurrency Control
lessons.description: Understand database transactions, ACID properties, isolation levels, locks and deadlocks.
lessons.content:
A transaction is a logical unit of database work containing one or more operations.

Example: Transferring 1000 from Account A to Account B requires deducting 1000 from A and adding 1000 to B.

Both operations should succeed together or be rolled back together.

ACID properties:

Atomicity:
A transaction is treated as one unit. Either its operations commit or its changes are rolled back.

Consistency:
A transaction preserves declared database integrity constraints when moving between valid states.

Isolation:
Concurrent transactions are controlled so their interactions follow the database's isolation guarantees.

Durability:
Once a transaction commits, its effects survive failures according to the DBMS durability guarantees.

Example transaction:
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 1000 WHERE AccountID = 1;
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 1000 WHERE AccountID = 2;
COMMIT;

In production, the application must also verify sufficient funds, affected row counts and transaction errors before committing.

Transaction commands:
COMMIT: Makes transaction changes permanent.
ROLLBACK: Reverts uncommitted transaction changes.
SAVEPOINT: Establishes a point for partial rollback where supported.

Concurrency problems:
Dirty Read: Reading another transaction's uncommitted changes.
Non-Repeatable Read: Reading the same row twice and observing a different committed value.
Phantom Read: Repeating a predicate query and observing a changed set of matching rows.
Lost Update: One transaction's update unintentionally overwrites another's update.

Common SQL isolation levels:
Read Uncommitted.
Read Committed.
Repeatable Read.
Serializable.

Exact behavior depends on the DBMS and its concurrency-control implementation.

Locks:
Shared locks are commonly used for reading protected data.
Exclusive locks are commonly used when modifying protected data.

Deadlock:
A deadlock occurs when transactions wait on resources held by one another and none can proceed without intervention.

Example:
Transaction T1 locks Row A and waits for Row B.
Transaction T2 locks Row B and waits for Row A.

Deadlock prevention and handling techniques include consistent lock ordering, shorter transactions, deadlock detection and retrying aborted transactions.

Interview question: What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

Answer: COMMIT finalizes a transaction's changes. ROLLBACK reverses uncommitted changes within the transaction.

lessons.title: Indexing, Query Optimization and DBMS Interview Preparation
lessons.description: Understand indexes, query performance, query plans and frequently asked DBMS interview concepts.
lessons.content:
An index is a database structure that helps locate records efficiently without scanning every row in suitable queries.

Common index types:
B-tree or B+ tree indexes: Useful for equality and range searches.
Hash indexes: Useful for equality searches in supported database systems.
Composite indexes: Include multiple columns.
Unique indexes: Enforce uniqueness of indexed key values according to DBMS rules.

Example:
CREATE INDEX idx_employee_department
ON Employees(DepartmentID);

This index may improve queries filtering or joining on DepartmentID.

Advantages:
1. Can speed up data retrieval.
2. Can improve filtering and join performance.
3. Can support sorting and grouping in suitable query plans.

Disadvantages:
1. Require storage space.
2. Increase maintenance work during inserts, updates and deletes.
3. May provide little benefit for certain queries.

Composite index example:
CREATE INDEX idx_department_salary
ON Employees(DepartmentID, Salary);

For many B-tree implementations, column order matters. An index on (DepartmentID, Salary) can be useful when queries filter by DepartmentID, but may not be equally useful for queries filtering only by Salary.

Query optimization is the process of choosing an efficient execution plan for a query.

Common optimization techniques:
1. Select only required columns.
2. Create appropriate indexes.
3. Avoid unnecessary joins.
4. Filter data efficiently.
5. Examine execution plans.
6. Avoid unnecessary repeated queries.
7. Use suitable data types.

EXPLAIN is commonly used to inspect query execution plans, although syntax and output vary by DBMS.

Example:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE DepartmentID = 10;

Important DBMS interview concepts:

Primary Key vs Unique Constraint:
A primary key uniquely identifies rows and disallows NULL values. Unique constraints enforce uniqueness, while NULL behavior varies by database system.

Clustered vs Nonclustered Index:
A clustered index determines or closely corresponds to the organization of table data in systems that support the distinction. A nonclustered index stores a separate lookup structure. Implementation details differ across database engines.

Stored Procedure:
A stored program containing database operations, supported with different syntax and capabilities across DBMS products.

Trigger:
A database routine executed automatically in response to specified database events.

View:
A query-defined database object used to present data through a reusable interface.

Interview preparation checklist:
1. DBMS vs RDBMS.
2. Keys and constraints.
3. ER diagrams and relationships.
4. Normalization and anomalies.
5. SQL joins and subqueries.
6. ACID properties.
7. Transactions and isolation levels.
8. Indexing and query optimization.
9. Deadlocks and concurrency.
10. Views, procedures and triggers.

Placement tip: For technical interviews, explain each concept using a simple database example rather than giving only a definition.

quizzes.question: What is the primary purpose of a DBMS?
quizzes.explanation: A DBMS stores, organizes, retrieves and manages data.

quizzes.question: Which key uniquely identifies each row in a relational table and cannot contain NULL values?
quizzes.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies every row and does not permit NULL values.

quizzes.question: Which normal form eliminates partial dependencies on a candidate key?
quizzes.explanation: Second Normal Form requires 1NF and full functional dependency of non-prime attributes on candidate keys.

quizzes.question: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation?
quizzes.explanation: HAVING filters grouped results, often using aggregate conditions.

quizzes.question: Which SQL join returns matching rows from both tables according to the join condition?
quizzes.explanation: INNER JOIN returns rows satisfying the join condition.

quizzes.question: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction is treated as a single unit of work?
quizzes.explanation: Atomicity ensures that a transaction's operations commit together or are rolled back.

quizzes.question: What is a dirty read?
quizzes.explanation: A dirty read occurs when a transaction observes changes made by another transaction before those changes commit.

quizzes.question: Which SQL command is used to make transaction changes permanent?
quizzes.explanation: COMMIT finalizes the transaction and makes its changes durable according to the database's guarantees.

quizzes.question: Which statement about database indexes is generally correct?
options: Indexes can improve retrieval but add maintenance overhead
Indexes eliminate the need for primary keys
quizzes.explanation: Indexes can speed up suitable queries but consume storage and require maintenance during data modifications.

quizzes.question: Transaction T1 holds Lock A and waits for Lock B. Transaction T2 holds Lock B and waits for Lock A. What situation has occurred?
quizzes.explanation: Both transactions are waiting on resources held by the other, creating a circular wait characteristic of deadlock.

exercises.title: Design a Student Database
exercises.description: Practice identifying entities, attributes, primary keys and foreign keys.
exercises.instructions: Design a database for a college containing Students, Departments and Courses. Identify attributes for each entity, select appropriate primary keys and explain how foreign keys establish relationships.

exercises.title: Database Normalization Challenge
exercises.description: Normalize a relational table and explain data anomalies.
exercises.instructions: Consider Enrollment(StudentID, StudentName, CourseID, CourseName, InstructorName), where StudentID determines StudentName and CourseID determines CourseName and InstructorName. Assume each course has one instructor. Decompose the table into a suitable normalized design and explain the functional dependencies and anomalies removed.

exercises.title: SQL Interview Query Practice
exercises.description: Write SQL queries using filtering, grouping, joins and subqueries.
exercises.instructions: Given Employees(EmployeeID, EmployeeName, Salary, DepartmentID) and Departments(DepartmentID, DepartmentName), write SQL queries to: (1) Find employees earning more than 50000. (2) Find the average salary per department. (3) Display employee names with department names. (4) Find employees earning above the company-wide average salary. (5) Find departments containing more than five employees.

exercises.title: Transaction and ACID Analysis
exercises.description: Explain transaction processing and concurrency problems using a banking example.
exercises.instructions: A banking application transfers 2000 from Account A to Account B. Explain how atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability apply. Describe what should happen if the second update fails, and give one example of a possible concurrency problem.

exercises.title: Advanced DBMS Interview Scenario
exercises.description: Analyze indexing, deadlocks and query performance in a realistic database scenario.
exercises.instructions: An application contains an Employees table with one million records. Queries frequently filter by DepartmentID and sort by Salary. Explain an appropriate indexing strategy and its trade-offs. Describe how to inspect the query execution plan. Then explain how two concurrent transactions could deadlock and suggest at least three ways to reduce or handle deadlocks.
